body_markdown:
Automotive history is rich with companies that began by building one thing and then pivoted to cars. Renzo Rivolta, for example, built refrigerators before he built cars (under the Iso name). Honda famously made its name on the saddles of small-bore motorbikes. In the German town of Dingolfing, meanwhile, if you needed machinery for your farm, Glas was your go-to. But while Iso had only been around for 15 years when it introduced the Isetta microcar, and Honda just 18 years when its T360 minitruck debuted, Glas had been a staple of Lower Bavaria for 72 years before its[first tiny, four-wheeled Goggomobil](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/cute-car-cute-name-it-was-impossible-to-not-love-the-goggomobil/) hit the road in 1955.


Just a decade later, the company was gone, absorbed by BMW, but the impact that Glas had on the microcar market can’t be overstated. And if you happen to be in the market for a microcar, this[1963 Goggomobil TS250](https://www.hagerty.com/marketplace/auction/1963-Goggomobil-TS250/533a6254-bf42-4116-921e-b45caa58441c) is up for sale right now on Hagerty Marketplace.


Hagerty Marketplace/David_Ross


Glas’s pivot to cars came after it first entered scooter production with the successful Goggo, an elegant art deco–inspired two-wheeler with a fully enclosed body made of stamped steel. As microcars became more prevalent throughout Europe, Glas considered designs for its own car, but rather than utilizing a single, front-mounted door[similar to that of the Isetta](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/exit-via-sunroof-and-other-tips-to-reorient-the-microcar-novice/) , or a side-hinged bubble canopy as found on Messerschmitts, the company opted for a three-box design with two doors, a hood, and a trunk. Glas wanted it to look like a car, in other words. Turns out the buying public approved.


The company’s first cars—the T250 sedan, TS250 coupe, and TL250 van—all featured stamped steel unibody construction and independent suspension, with a rear-mounted, 247-cc air-cooled two-stroke twin making 13 horsepower, which was mated to a four-speed manual transmission that drove the rear, 10-inch wheels.


Hagerty Marketplace/David_Ross


Hagerty Marketplace/David_Ross


Displacement grew over the next few years, to 296 cc and then 392 cc, with subsequent model names reflecting the added size—e.g., T300, T400. There was even a 682-cc four-stroke model, the T700, introduced for 1959. Goggomobils were immensely popular in Europe, though a small number made their way to the States, too, between 1955 and 1961, courtesy of New York’s Continental Car Combine.


Glas began dabbling in Frua-bodied full-size GTs in the early 1960s, but the move upmarket proved its undoing, and BMW took control in 1966. Goggomobil production continued through 1969, however, by which time nearly 280,000 had been built.

The TS250 currently offered on Hagerty Marketplace features a black roof over a cream body, with a red interior. The listing states the car lived for some time in a British museum as a running exhibit, where it was refurbished at some point. The consignor brought it to the U.S. and has owned it for six years.


As of this writing, bidding currently sits at $1100, and the auction ends October 7. If you fancy a microcar to add to your garage, or even the closet in your garage, perhaps this Goggomobil is calling your name?
